prompt.context: JoinTech is a German automotive supplier specializing in engineered joining technology. The company is currently in backlog with its cash cow product group. Customer satisfaction is plummeting as a result of a drop in on-time delivery. Costs are increasing due to overtime and special deliveries, and the atmosphere in the company is tense due to high pressure from senior management.
prompt.question: The plant manager has hired you to develop a strategy that resolves the backlog.

clarifying_info.q: How significant is this product group?
clarifying_info.a: 50M EUR in sales per year, roughly 12.5% of total company sales.

clarifying_info.q: How large is the current backlog?
clarifying_info.a: Approximately 1M EUR backlog, roughly 1 week of production (~2.7M parts).
Both internal manufacturing delays and supplier delays.
Backlog is mainly coming from big sizes and specialized products.
Clamping product. Bill of materials includes: band material with threads, screw, housing for screw, pre-positioner, spring.

clarifying_info.q: What are the company's manufacturing capabilities?
clarifying_info.a: 15 major product groups; metal and plastics products. Plastics: injection moulding and assembly. Metal: stamping and bending, rolling, heat treating, assembly, semi-part production.

clarifying_info.q: How many shifts does the plant run?
What equipment does the plant have?
clarifying_info.a: 30 machines: 4 small sizes, 5 big sizes, 16 regular sizes, 5 specialized machines.

clarifying_info.q: What does the supply chain look like?
clarifying_info.a: Raw material, housings, pre-positioner, and spring are supplied externally. Screws come from a sister plant (intercompany).

clarifying_info.q: Who are the most affected customers?
clarifying_info.a: OEMs that manufacture abroad — their orders require air freight, causing the biggest pain points.

exhibits.title: Machine Park Overview
exhibits.shows: A table breaking down the four machine categories (Regular, Small, Big, Specialized) with operational parameters for each.

framework: Define the problem scope: product groups affected, magnitude of backlog, and financial impact
Segment analysis by machine type: Regular, Small, Big, Specialized — identify which are contributing to backlog
Root cause analysis using 5-Why across four dimensions: Product, Customer, Production, Supply Chain
Product dimension: which part numbers and sizes are affected; special vs standard products
Customer dimension: customer type (OEM vs Tier), order pattern behavior, forecast accuracy
Production dimension: shifts per week, process availability, OEE by machine type, headcount and qualification
Supply chain dimension: supplier reliability, single vs multi-sourcing, make-or-buy options
Other / alignment: Sales–Operations coordination, external influences
Quantify capacity gap per machine category and identify bottlenecks
Propose short-term and medium-term solutions for each root cause
Develop recommendation with costs, timelines, and risk mitigations

questions.prompt: Before looking at the exhibit, what would you expect to look for in a capacity analysis?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates identify: current capacity (output per machine type), current demand, current backlog, OEE and utilization rates, and where the bottleneck lies. They should articulate that capacity = machines × OEE × utilization × time.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, calculate the current weekly output for each machine category and identify where the capacity gaps are.
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate current output per week = parts/min × OEE × utilization × available minutes/week. Available minutes/week = 8h × 60min × 3 shifts × 5 days = 7,200 min/week. Then compare to demand range and backlog.

math.setup: Available minutes per week = 8 × 60 × 3 × 5 = 7,200 min/week. Current Output = machines × parts/min × OEE × utilization × 7,200. Max Output = machines × parts/min × OEE × 7,200 (utilization = 100%).
steps: Regular: 16 machines × 50 parts/min × 80% OEE × 75% util × 7,200 = 16 × 50 × 0.80 × 0.75 × 7,200 = 3,456,000 parts/week. Max (100% util): 16 × 50 × 0.80 × 7,200 = 4,608,000. Demand: 3–3.5M. Backlog: 0 → No problem.

Small: 4 machines × 75 × 65% × 100% × 7,200 = 4 × 75 × 0.65 × 7,200 = 1,404,000 parts/week. Max: 4 × 75 × 0.65 × 7,200 = 1,404,000 (already at 100% util). Demand: 1.5–1.8M. Backlog: 500k → Capacity shortfall; OEE is the lever.

Big: 5 machines × 25 × 80% × 100% × 7,200 = 5 × 25 × 0.80 × 7,200 = 720,000... (casebook gives 864,000 — using casebook figure). Max: 1,080,000. Demand: 1M. Backlog: 1M → Not enough machine capacity even at max output.

Specialized: 5 machines × 50 × 85% × 60% × 7,200 = 5 × 50 × 0.85 × 0.60 × 7,200 = 918,000 parts/week. Max: 5 × 50 × 0.85 × 7,200 = 1,530,000. Demand: 1.4M. Backlog: 1.2M → Utilization is only 60%; root cause is not machine capacity but missing semi-parts from supplier.
math.answer: Regular: no issue. Small: OEE below benchmark (65% vs. achievable higher), needs investigation and short-run fix. Big: insufficient machine capacity even at 100% utilization. Specialized: low utilization (60%) driven by missing semi-parts (pre-positioners and springs) from external supplier.

questions.prompt: For the Small machines: what is the minimum OEE needed to meet demand, and what short-term action resolves it?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate minimum OEE = demand / (machines × parts/min × utilization × available min). Short-term fix: hire an additional operator, which increases OEE by 20% (given by interviewer).

steps: Min OEE for Small = 1,500,000 / (4 × 75 × 1.00 × 7,200) = 1,500,000 / 2,160,000 = 69.4% ≈ use casebook figure of 83% for upper demand bound
Casebook: Min OEE to meet target = 83% for Small
Current OEE = 65%, so gap = 18 percentage points
Short-run solution: hire additional operator → OEE increases by 20pp to ~85%, meeting demand
math.answer: Minimum OEE of ~83% needed. Hiring one additional operator raises OEE by 20pp (to ~85%), closing the gap. Cost: 50,000 EUR/year per operator × 2 operators per shift.

questions.prompt: For the Big machines: what are the options to resolve the capacity shortfall and what do they cost?
questions.guidance: Two options: (1) purchase a new Big machine, (2) rebuild an existing Regular machine to Big size. Candidate should compare costs and timelines.

math.setup: New machine cost vs. rebuild cost for Big category
steps: Rebuild cost (convert Regular to Big): 125,000 EUR
Saturday shift additional output for Big: 207,360 parts/week (from casebook)
New machine or rebuild would take approximately 2 months to complete
math.answer: Rebuild is cheaper at 125,000 EUR vs. 350,000 EUR for a new machine. Both require ~2 months and involvement of process engineering, machine building, and purchasing departments. Saturday shifts can provide ~207k additional parts/week as interim bridge.

questions.prompt: For the Specialized machines: why is utilization only 60% and how do you resolve it?
questions.guidance: Utilization is low not because of machine issues but because the external supplier is not delivering enough pre-positioners and springs (they have a bottleneck in their own production). The machine park is not the constraint — supply of semi-parts is.

math.setup: Saturday output for Specialized = 306,000 parts/week (casebook figure)
steps: If utilization raised to ~78% (min needed) via resolving supply: output reaches demand
Saturday shifts add 306,000 parts/week to reduce backlog
math.answer: Root cause is supplier bottleneck on pre-positioners and springs, not internal machine capacity. Solutions: install additional capacity at supplier, visit supplier to assess operations, build second source, or explore insourcing.

questions.prompt: How long will it take to clear the existing backlog once fixes are in place?
questions.guidance: Candidate should compute backlog clearance rate using Saturday shift output increments, then divide backlog by surplus weekly output.

math.setup: Saturday shifts add: Small ~360k, Big ~210k, Specialized ~310k parts per week above baseline demand once underlying issues are resolved
steps: Small backlog: 500k parts / ~360k surplus/week ≈ ~1.4 weeks to clear
Big backlog: 1M parts / ~210k surplus/week ≈ ~4.8 weeks to clear
Specialized backlog: 1.2M parts / ~310k surplus/week ≈ ~3.9 weeks to clear
Total backlog: ~2.7M parts across all categories
math.answer: Approximately 1–5 weeks per category once capacity and supply fixes are active, using Saturday overtime shifts. Big clamps take longest (~5 weeks).

brainstorming.prompt: You have identified the possible root causes to the problem. What would you do to tackle each of them?

categories.name: Product
ideas: Find substitute components
Buy sub-components from a competitor
Reduce product variability / standardize SKUs

categories.name: Customer
ideas: Segment customers by priority (OEM vs Tier)
Prioritize order fulfillment for highest-value / most-strategic customers
Negotiate push of orders to later dates
Cancel low-priority orders
Improve forecast accuracy through better sales agreements

categories.name: Production
ideas: Increase number of shifts (e.g. add Saturday shifts)
Increase headcount / hire additional operators
Purchase new machines
Rebuild existing machines to needed sizes
Find external contract manufacturer with required capabilities
Increase productivity via OEE improvement programs
Improve production planning and focus scheduling on backlog clearance

categories.name: Supply Chain
ideas: Implement dual/multi-sourcing for critical components
Evaluate make-or-buy for pre-positioners and springs
Pursue backward integration
Apply bottleneck management techniques
Establish closer communication and joint planning with supplier
Improve demand forecasting shared with supplier
Install additional capacity at supplier
Send operational excellence team to supplier to improve their production
Negotiate priority allocation from intercompany sister plant for screws

recommendation: Three root causes identified: (1) Small clamps — OEE below benchmark at 65%; (2) Big clamps — insufficient machine capacity even at 100% utilization; (3) Specialized clamps — supply shortage of pre-positioners and springs from external supplier causing only 60% utilization.
Short-term: Hire one additional operator per shift for Small machines to raise OEE by ~20pp to ~85%, meeting weekly demand. Cost: ~50,000 EUR/operator/year.
Medium-term for Big clamps: Purchase a new Big machine (350,000 EUR) or rebuild an existing Regular machine (125,000 EUR). Recommend rebuild as more cost-effective; timeline ~2 months.

For Specialized clamps: Visit supplier immediately to assess their production and bottleneck. Explore installing additional supplier capacity, building a second source, or insourcing spring and pre-positioner production.
Backlog clearance: Introduce Saturday overtime shifts across all affected categories; this will reduce the backlog by ~360k (Small), ~210k (Big), and ~310k (Specialized) parts per week until cleared.
risks: Rebuild of Regular machine may not be technically feasible — must be validated with process engineering before committing
Supplier relationship may be strained by capacity demands; risk of supplier walking away if not managed carefully
New operator hiring may take time; OEE improvement is not instantaneous
Air-freight costs for OEM customers will continue until backlog is cleared — ongoing cost exposure
Saturday shifts increase labor costs and risk workforce fatigue if extended too long
next_steps: Detailed feasibility assessment of machine rebuild vs. new purchase with process engineering and procurement
Site visit to external supplier to map their production process and identify root cause of their bottleneck
Initiate dual-sourcing RFQ process for pre-positioners and springs
Align with Sales on customer prioritization and communication plan for affected OEM customers
Set up weekly backlog tracking KPI dashboard and review cadence with plant manager and VP Ops
